Title: (D) Bleeds vs. non-prey ... Where is it written

Messages.Author: Mike Kelly
Messages.Body:

They then showed me in print where it said this is legal. Where is this ruling

this debate, but a long running "Are CTB (cross table bleeds) legal?"

From: aa...@cats.ucsc.edu (Thomas R Wylie)
Newsgroups: rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad
Subject: *NEW* Official FAQ for Jyhad, April 95 version
Date: 13 Apr 1995 01:16:26 GMT
Message-Id: <3mhu1a$h...@darkstar.UCSC.EDU>

Q: Who do you bleed? And if I have a card with the D in the
circle, who then? And wasn't bleeding a direct action anyway?
A: Usually the only one you bleed is your prey. That action is
direct, that is, it can only be blocked by your prey. If,
however, a card allows you to bleed as a directed action, then you
can bleed any Methuselah you like. It's still a direct action, so
only the target of the bleed can attempt to block.

However, this stance (an false assumption that (D) imparts omni-directability)
leads to many false conclusions (proof by contradiction that (D) is just
a reminder).

<Note: the (D) symbol only means that an action is directed, so the

In Murk Dwellers of Duelist 6 Tom Wylie states:

'The official ruling is that the general rule for directed actions
such as Computer Hacking overrides the implicit exception given for
bleed actions.'

Thus a (D) bleed can be used against any methuselah, but in the same
article:

'The question is: Should you be able to direct (D) bleeds at any
player? ... The Duelist invites your comments on this issue.'

So *at the moment* (D) bleeds against any player are allowed.

Not quite, in summary:

1) Bleeding is a directed action, which means it can only be blocked
by the methuselah that is the target.

2) Bleeding is a special exception to the directed action rule, in
that it can only be targeted on your prey.

3) All (D)-rated directed actions can be tageted at any methuselah.

4) If a bleed modifier is played (eg computer hacking, (D) bleed +1),
which is a (D) action, then condition 3 applies. If no cards are
played which say the action is (D), then condition 2 applies.
In either case, condition 1 applies.

I hope this is clearer, but read the article if possible.

But it can easily be argued that since (D) actions have the symbol, and
since bleeds are cardless and yet are still directed (and hence (D)
actions) that they can be directed at anyone.

As of now, (D) bleeds allow CTB, but whether or not that is what was
intended or what should be is unclear. IMHO, the game itself doesn't
suffer in either avenue. If (D) bleeds are written to allow CTB, the
rulebook needs to be rewritten, and if CTB is not allowed, this needs to
be clarified (i.e., the rulebook needs to be rewritten).

> I hope this is clearer, but read the article if possible.

This issue has never been clear. I have always played CTB, because that
seemed most intuitively obvious. However, after reading numerous
articles on CTB, playing without CTB seems far more logical as the rules
are written. In any case, I hope things improve. This will only happen
if the rulebook is rewritten to logically included CTB or if the DTR
reverses its ruling.

Messages.Author: L. Scott Johnson
Messages.Body:
Ubermensch <kfin...@netshop.net> writes:

>Please hear me out.

>I would like to know what the OFFICIAL WOtC standpoint on Directed
>Bleeds is -- ie. how did the designers INTEND it to work? Can you bleed
>anyone with a Computer Hacking, Govern The Unaligned, et al? Or are you
>restricted to your prey as target, except in those cases where the card
>says otherwise (Cat Burglary, Night Moves)?

The official standpoint and how the designers intended for it to be
are two different things. When the game was being developed, the (D)
symbols was a reminder. At some point (arguably before the game was
released), the Design Team changed it to be omni-directability-granting,
thus allowing Computer Hacking to target any /other/ Methuselah while
breaking cards like Cat Burglary and making Night Moves slightly less
useful in comparison.

>All I've seen on this NG is debate and (outright) bickering. Can we get
>an answer from THE AUTHORITY on Jyhad/V:TES?

Every debate has started with an acknowledgement of the official
WayOfTheWorld (WOTW).

in the following way:

A directed action is one which only the targeted Methusaleh may block.

A cardless bleed is a special directed action which may only be taken

Getting away from (D) as a reminder... Well, whether or not that is a
good thing, the jury is out.

> If you add who the directed action can be targeted at into the
> definition, then yes, it looks good, and would probably eliminate debate.

See above.

If I had my way (if only :), I think I would change the whole of
(D)-actions. Note that these are contradictory to "real" rulings.

"Controlled": Not to be confused with controlled region, all of the
cards/counters that the Methuselah has direct power over.

1) Any action that exclusively affects another Methuselah or the cards
"controlled" by that Methuselah is a directed action. Note that votes
call a referendum and are thus not directed, while putting Charnas on an
opposing vampire would be.
(I.e., If you point an action at someone, it is directed)
2) Any action that affects the acting Methuselah or not any single
Methuselah is undirected.
(I.e., If you point at yourself or no _one_ Methuselah, it is
undirected)
3) (D) actions can be performed against oneself (if not explicitly
disallowed such as by Night Moves or Bum's Rush), and thus become undirected.

I feel these rules work with one of the following (depending on your view
of CTB).

4a) Cards that allow (D) actions allow you to target any Methuselah,
limited by card text. (Pro-CTB)
4b) Cards that allow (D) actions explicitly tell you who can be
targetted, or if they don't are governed by normal rules for that
action. (No-CTB)

Though some might think otherwise, every card that describes a (D) action
(with the exception of bleeds) describes who the action may be directed
against, so 4b is as viable with the cards as 4a.

Any thoughts?

>Any thoughts?

This is nearly perfect (ObQual).

It can be summed up as (the original, RCG, intent):

1. All actions have explicit targets, by rules text or card text.
2. If an action targets another (single) Methuselah (any permanents she
controls - pool, minion, locations, etc.) then it is directed.
3. If not, then it is not directed.

To make the game work the way the RTR tries to wring out of the rules which
do not support them, add:

4. An action card decribing a bleed may target any other Methuselah
((D)-symbol-as-overriding-card-text) unless further card text (or errata)
restricts this (Cat Burglary, Night Moves). This overriding card text only
overrides rules text, and will not override other card text (Minor Boon).

Micro-sum:

1. All actions can only target valid targets.
2. Actions are directed or not based on whether they target another Meth.

These two rules are so obvious to be almost circular definitions.
But the Rules Team doesn't agree with the simplicity. (cf. Shackles of
Endiku, The Treatment).

Optional (CTB):
3. Carded bleeds can target otherwise invalid targets.

----
Note that no action targets more than one Methuselah, except some
(actually, all) votes - which target all Methuselahs (calling them
to the quorum) and therefore cannot be considered directed (that,
and explicit rules text :-).
